At arm's length in front
Overhead
At the side in one hand
e: Holding the bell tight to the sternum creates a forward moment the trunk resists, which keeps the chest up and lets the hips sit down between the knees. Moving it away from the body increases the demand disproportionately and usually breaks the position.

q: In a cable triceps pushdown, what is the fault that changes the exercise?
o: Letting the upper arm drift forward and back, which brings the lats and shoulder into it
Standing too close to the stack
Using a rope rather than a bar
Extending the elbow fully at the bottom
e: Only the elbow should move. If the humerus swings, the shoulder is extending too and the lats contribute, which is a different exercise that happens to be easier. Pinning the upper arm to the ribs is the whole setup.

q: In a standing curl, what is the giveaway that the shoulder is doing the work?
o: The elbow travelling forward as the weight rises
The wrist staying straight
The knees being soft
The grip being supinated
e: The biceps flexes the shoulder as well as the elbow, so when the load gets heavy the elbow drifts forward and the shoulder takes over. Keeping the elbow beside the ribs is what confines the movement to one joint.

q: In a face pull, where should the hands finish?
o: Level with or above the eyes, with the hands ending outside the elbows
At chest height with the hands inside the elbows
At the waist
Behind the head
e: The point is combining horizontal abduction with external rotation. Finishing high with the hands outside the elbows produces both. Pulling to the chest with the hands low makes it an ordinary row and loses the rotation entirely.

q: In a dumbbell lateral raise, what does turning the thumb down do?
o: Internally rotates the shoulder while abducting it, which narrows the subacromial space
Increases the lateral deltoid's leverage safely
Recruits the supraspinatus more effectively
Reduces trapezius involvement
e: The pouring cue is widespread and it recreates the impingement position under load. Keeping the thumb level or slightly up loads the same muscle without putting the shoulder in the position that pinches.

q: In an assisted pull-up, what is the most common setup error?
o: Selecting so much assistance that the target muscles barely work
Kneeling rather than standing on the pad
Using a neutral grip
Holding the top position
e: The weight stack is counterweight: more plates means an easier rep. It is the one machine where a heavier selection makes the exercise lighter, which is the mistake almost everyone makes on their first attempt.

q: Machines only, and the target is the rhomboids and middle trapezius. Which machine and which setting?
o: A seated row, pulling with the elbows high and wide
A seated row with the elbows tucked low
A lat pulldown with a wide grip
A chest press machine
e: Elbows high and wide makes the movement horizontal abduction with scapular retraction, which is what the mid-back muscles do. Tucking the elbows on the same machine biases the lats instead, so the setting matters more than the machine.

q: Machines only, and the aim is pectoralis major with the elbow excluded. Which one?
o: A chest fly machine with the elbows fixed on pads
A chest press machine
An assisted dip machine
A cable pushdown
e: Fixing the elbow angle leaves the shoulder as the only moving joint, so the triceps cannot contribute. Any pressing machine involves elbow extension by design, which is the difference between a press and a fly.

q: Which machine trains the hip flexors, and why is it uncommon?
o: A cable stack with an ankle strap, flexing the hip against resistance; few gyms have a dedicated hip flexor machine
The leg extension, since it flexes the hip
The leg press at a high foot position
The hip adduction machine
e: Resisted hip flexion needs a cable and a strap in most gyms. The leg extension moves the knee, not the hip, and neither of the others flexes it. The hip flexors are among the least catered-for muscle groups on a standard gym floor.

q: Which machine would you use for the erector spinae working dynamically?
o: A back extension bench, allowing the spine to flex and extend through range
A seated row with a chest pad
A leg press
An abdominal crunch machine
e: Moving the spine into extension against gravity is what loads the erectors concentrically. A chest-supported row deliberately removes them, and the crunch machine trains the opposite action.

q: Only a cable stack is available and the target is the gluteus maximus. What setup?
o: A cable kickback or a cable pull-through, both producing resisted hip extension
A cable curl
A cable lateral raise
A cable rotation
e: Glute max extends the hip, so the resistance has to oppose hip extension. A pull-through gives a hinge pattern against the stack; a kickback isolates it. Neither is as loadable as a hip thrust, but both work with one machine.

q: Which machine best trains the triceps with the shoulder in flexion rather than neutral?
o: A cable stack used for an overhead extension
A cable pushdown
An assisted dip machine
A chest press machine
e: Shoulder position decides how much the long head is stretched. Overhead puts it at length before the set; a pushdown keeps the arm at the side. Same muscle, different starting length, which is the reason to include both.

q: A client needs the lats but cannot grip a bar because of a hand injury. What machine option remains?
o: A pullover machine or a lat pulldown with cuffs, which load the shoulder without gripping
A seated row with a thick handle
An assisted pull-up
A cable curl
e: Both remaining options transmit force through the elbow or upper arm rather than the hand. Any rowing or pulling movement held by the fingers is out, which is a common constraint and one machines happen to solve well.

q: Which machine loads the hamstrings eccentrically with the least skill required?
o: A seated or lying leg curl, lowering the weight slowly
A back extension bench
A leg press
The hip adduction machine
e: The leg curl's fixed path means the only variable is tempo, so lengthening under load is just a matter of lowering slowly. A Nordic curl trains the same thing far harder but needs technique and a tolerance most beginners do not have.

q: Which machine setting would you change first if a client feels a lat pulldown entirely in their arms?
o: Cue the elbows to drive down and back rather than the hands to pull, before changing anything on the machine
Increase the weight to force the lats to work
Widen the grip as far as the bar allows
Raise the thigh pad
e: The lats move the upper arm, so thinking about where the elbow goes recruits them; thinking about the hands recruits the elbow flexors. It is a cueing fix rather than a machine fix, which is worth trying before touching the settings.

q: Which machine most closely reproduces the demand of a farmer's carry?
o: None of them; the demand is bracing and holding under load while walking, which no fixed machine reproduces
The shrug machine
The seated row
The cable stack with heavy handles
e: A shrug loads the traps and a row loads the back, but neither asks the trunk to stay stacked while moving under an external load. Some qualities are only trainable away from machines, and this is one of the clearest examples.

q: Which machine would you select to train knee extension for a client who cannot bear weight through the leg?
o: The leg extension, since it is non weight-bearing and seated
The leg press
The hack squat
The Smith machine squat
e: Bearing weight is exactly what the other three require. A leg extension loads the knee with the body supported, which is why it appears so often in early rehabilitation despite being an unfashionable exercise.

q: Which two machines together cover both functions of the hamstrings?
o: A leg curl for the knee action and a back extension or hip thrust machine for the hip action
A leg curl and a leg extension
A leg press and a hip adduction machine
A hack squat and a calf machine
e: The hamstrings flex the knee and extend the hip. A curl covers the first and a hip extension movement covers the second. Training only one leaves half the group's function untouched, which is the argument against relying on the curl alone.

q: Rowing machine: what is the correct sequence of the drive?
o: Legs, then hips and back, then arms
Arms, then back, then legs
Legs and arms together, then the back
Back, then legs, then arms
e: The strongest segment goes first and the weakest last. Legs drive the seat back, the hips and trunk swing open, and only then do the arms finish the pull. Reversing it means the arms try to move a load the legs should have shifted.

q: Rowing machine: roughly how is the work distributed?
o: About sixty per cent legs, thirty per cent hips and back, ten per cent arms
About sixty per cent arms, thirty per cent back, ten per cent legs
Evenly across legs, back and arms
Almost entirely the back
e: It reads as an upper-body machine because that is where the handle is, but it is a leg press with a pull attached. People who feel rowing entirely in their arms and grip are almost always sequencing it backwards.

q: Rowing machine: what is the most common fault on the recovery?
o: Bending the knees before the handle has passed them, so the handle has to travel over them
Straightening the arms too early
Leaning forward too late
Keeping the back too upright
e: The recovery reverses the drive: arms away, then hinge forward, then bend the knees. Breaking the knees early puts them in the handle's path, which forces an awkward lift over the top and wastes the stroke.

q: Stationary bike: how should the saddle height be set?
o: So the knee retains a slight bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke, roughly twenty-five to thirty-five degrees
So the leg fully straightens at the bottom
So the knee stays at ninety degrees throughout
So the rider can place both feet flat on the floor while seated
e: Too low and the knee never opens, which loads the front of the joint and limits power. Too high and the hips rock side to side reaching for the pedal. A small residual bend at the bottom is the target, and it is the single most commonly wrong setting in any gym.

q: Stationary bike: what does a saddle set too high produce?
o: Rocking hips and strain at the back of the knee
Pain at the front of the knee
An inability to reach the handlebars
Excessive quadriceps fatigue only
e: Reaching for the bottom of the stroke makes the pelvis tip side to side and overextends the knee, which stresses the hamstring attachment behind it. A saddle too low does the opposite and irritates the front of the knee.

q: Treadmill: what does raising the incline do to the muscular demand?
o: Increases the demand on the hip extensors, the glutes and hamstrings
Increases the demand on the anterior tibialis
Reduces the demand on the calf complex
Shifts the work to the quadriceps only
e: Climbing requires more hip extension to drive the body upward, so the glutes and hamstrings do more. It is also a way of raising intensity without raising speed, which matters for anyone whose joints do not tolerate faster running.

q: Treadmill: what is wrong with holding the handrails?
o: It offloads bodyweight, so the work done is less than the display suggests
It improves posture but reduces balance training
It has no effect beyond comfort
It increases the cardiovascular demand
e: Leaning on the rails transfers part of the body's weight into the arms, so both the muscular and the metabolic cost fall. The machine has no way of knowing, so the calorie and workload readouts become fiction.

q: Stair climber: which muscle group does it emphasise compared with a flat treadmill walk?
o: The hip extensors, especially gluteus maximus
The anterior tibialis
The adductors
The latissimus dorsi
e: Stepping up is repeated hip and knee extension against bodyweight, which is why it is felt in the glutes. Flat walking has far less hip extension range and demand per step.

q: Elliptical: what is its defining characteristic?
o: A fixed low-impact path, which reduces joint loading and also reduces the balance demand
A free path that trains coordination
Greater muscular demand than running
A purely upper-body stimulus
e: The feet never leave the pedals, so impact is low and the stride is dictated by the machine. That makes it useful when impact must be limited, and less useful when the aim is running-specific carry-over.

q: Assault or air bike: what distinguishes it from a standard stationary bike?
o: The arms drive as well as the legs, so more total muscle mass is working
It uses magnetic rather than air resistance
It cannot be used seated
It loads the arms only
e: Moving handles mean the upper body contributes, which raises the metabolic cost sharply for the same leg effort. The fan also means resistance rises with effort, so it self-scales rather than needing a level selected.

q: Ski erg: which muscles does the pulling action emphasise?
o: The latissimus dorsi and triceps, with the trunk flexing to assist
The biceps and anterior deltoid
The quadriceps
The rotator cuff
e: Pulling from overhead down past the hips is shoulder extension plus elbow extension, which is lats and triceps. The trunk contributes by flexing, which is why it is felt in the abdominals as much as the arms.

q: A client wants a cardio machine that loads the hip extensors and tolerates a sore knee. What fits best?
o: An inclined treadmill walk
A stair climber
A rowing machine at high resistance
A leg press performed quickly
e: Incline walking increases hip extension demand without the repeated deep knee flexion of stair climbing or the compressive load of rowing hard. The last option is not a cardio machine at all.

q: What happens to a resistance band's tension through the range?
o: It increases as the band stretches, so the exercise is hardest at the end range
It stays constant throughout
It decreases as the band stretches
It peaks in the middle of the range
e: Elastic resistance is a function of how far it has been stretched. That makes bands useful where the muscle is strongest at the short end, and a poor match where the hardest part of the lift is at the start.

q: What is the defining property of cable resistance compared with a free weight?
o: The line of pull can be set in any direction, and tension stays roughly constant through the range
It increases through the range like a band
It requires more stabiliser work than a dumbbell
It only works vertically
e: A free weight always pulls straight down, so the difficulty depends on the limb's angle to gravity. A cable pulls toward the pulley wherever that is, which is why it can load positions gravity cannot reach.

q: Why is a dumbbell lateral raise hardest when the arm is horizontal?
o: The moment arm between the shoulder and the weight is longest there
The deltoid is at its weakest length there
The supraspinatus disengages at that point
Gravity acts more strongly at that height
e: The load always falls straight down, so the torque at the shoulder depends on how far the weight is horizontally from the joint. At shoulder height that distance is at its maximum, which is why the last part of the raise feels disproportionately hard.

q: Why is a barbell curl hardest at about ninety degrees of elbow flexion?
o: The forearm is horizontal there, so the moment arm at the elbow is longest
The biceps is fully shortened there
The brachialis disengages at that angle
The wrist flexors take over past that point
e: Same principle as the lateral raise. Torque is the weight multiplied by its horizontal distance from the joint, and that distance peaks when the moving segment is parallel to the floor. Nothing about the muscle changes; the leverage does.

q: Where is a squat hardest, and why?
o: Near the bottom, where the hips and knees are most flexed and the moment arms are longest
At the top, where the bar is highest
In the middle, where speed is greatest
At the point where the knees pass the toes
e: Depth increases the horizontal distance from the bar to both the hip and the knee, which is what makes the torque demand peak there. It is also why partial squats allow so much more weight without training the hard part.

q: How does a well-designed machine cam try to improve on a free weight?
o: By varying the resistance through the range to match the strength curve of the movement
By removing the eccentric phase
By increasing resistance continuously like a band
By eliminating the need to stabilise
e: A free weight is hardest where the leverage is worst, not where the muscle is strongest. A cam alters the effective load through the range to fit the muscle better. Whether any given machine succeeds is a separate question.

q: What does a dumbbell bench press offer over a barbell version?
o: A greater range of motion and more stabiliser demand, at the cost of absolute load
More absolute load for the same effort
Less shoulder involvement
A fixed path that is easier to learn
e: The hands are free, so they can travel lower than a bar would allow and must be controlled independently. That is more range and more demand on the small stabilising muscles, and it is why the same person presses less with dumbbells.

q: Why can a kettlebell be swung in ways a dumbbell cannot?
o: The mass hangs below and away from the handle, which suits ballistic and rotational movements
It is always heavier
It has a fixed centre of mass at the handle
It cannot be used for slow lifts
e: The offset centre of mass creates an arc and a pendulum effect, which is what makes swings, cleans and snatches work. A dumbbell's mass sits in line with the hand, which suits controlled lifting rather than ballistics.

q: What does adding chains or bands to a barbell achieve?
o: Accommodating resistance: the load increases as the lift progresses into its stronger range
A reduction in load at the top of the lift
A constant load with less bar whip
An increase in stabiliser demand only
e: Most lifts are weakest at the bottom and strongest near lockout, so a constant barbell load underloads the top. Chains lift off the floor and bands stretch as the bar rises, adding resistance where there is capacity for it.

q: A client cannot load a movement heavily but needs a challenge at the end range. What implement suits?
o: A band, which is hardest where it is most stretched
A dumbbell
A kettlebell
A weight stack machine with a cam
e: The band's ascending profile puts the hardest part where the muscle is short, which is exactly the end range. It is why bands suit things like glute bridges and external rotation work where the top is otherwise trivially easy.

q: Why does a cable lateral raise feel different from a dumbbell one?
o: The cable maintains tension at the bottom, where a dumbbell's moment arm is nearly zero
The cable is heavier at the top
The cable removes the supraspinatus
The cable changes the prime mover
e: With the arm hanging, a dumbbell produces almost no torque at the shoulder because it sits directly under the joint. A cable pulling from the side keeps loading it there, which is why the bottom of the range suddenly has something to do.

q: Sumo against conventional deadlift: what changes?
o: Sumo gives a more upright torso, a shorter bar path and more adductor and quadriceps involvement
Sumo increases spinal loading and range
Conventional removes the hamstrings
They are mechanically identical
e: The wide stance lowers the hips, shortens the distance the bar travels and turns the femurs out, which brings the adductors in and reduces the forward lean. Neither is easier in general; they suit different proportions.

q: High-bar against low-bar back squat: what changes?
o: Low bar allows more forward lean and more hip contribution; high bar keeps the torso upright and loads the knees more
High bar increases hip involvement
Low bar removes the quadriceps
Bar position changes only comfort
e: Where the bar sits determines the torso angle needed to keep it over the midfoot. Further down the back means more lean and a longer moment arm at the hip. Same exercise name, meaningfully different distribution.

q: Leg press against hack squat: what is the practical difference?
o: The hack squat keeps the torso upright and the body moving, which feels closer to a squat; the leg press keeps the back supported and the body fixed
The leg press loads the hamstrings and the hack squat does not
They load entirely different muscles
The hack squat removes the quadriceps
e: Both extend the knee and hip against a fixed path. The difference is orientation and how much of the body moves, which affects comfort and spinal loading more than it affects which muscles work.

q: Pull-up against lat pulldown: what is the substantive difference?
o: The pull-up moves the body toward a fixed bar and cannot be loaded below bodyweight without assistance
The pulldown trains different muscles
The pull-up removes the biceps
The pulldown allows no scapular movement
e: The muscle actions are the same. What differs is what moves and how the load is set: the pulldown lets you select anything from very light upward, while the pull-up starts at your bodyweight and needs a machine or a band to go lower.

q: Seated row against bent-over barbell row: what does the seated version remove?
o: The demand on the erectors and hips to hold a hinged position under load
The latissimus dorsi
The biceps
The scapular retractors
e: The pulling is much the same. Sitting with the chest supported removes the isometric back and hip work that makes the bent-over version fatiguing well beyond the muscles being trained.

q: Front squat against back squat: which is more limited by upper-back strength?
o: The front squat, since the load must be held in front and resists trunk flexion
The back squat, because the bar sits on the traps
Neither; both are limited by the legs
Both equally
e: A front-racked bar constantly tries to pull the torso forward, so the thoracic extensors and the rack position often fail before the legs do. It is why many people front squat considerably less than they back squat.

q: Incline against flat dumbbell press: what actually changes?
o: The angle of the humerus to the torso, which shifts emphasis toward the clavicular pec and anterior deltoid
The muscles involved change completely
The triceps are removed
The range of motion decreases
e: Pec major inserts at one point but originates along the clavicle, sternum and ribs. Changing the torso angle changes which fibres are best aligned with the movement, and tilting up also brings the movement closer to shoulder flexion.

q: Goblet squat against back squat for a beginner: what is the argument for the goblet?
o: The front-loaded position self-corrects trunk posture and limits the load to what can be held
It loads the legs more heavily
It removes the need for ankle mobility
It trains different muscles
e: Holding weight at the chest makes rounding forward difficult and caps the load at what the arms can support, which is usually well within what the back can tolerate. It teaches the pattern with a built-in safety limit.

q: A client cannot perform a full push-up. What is the first regression to try?
o: Raise the hands onto a bench or box, reducing the proportion of bodyweight carried
Drop to the knees immediately
Reduce the range to the top few inches
Move to a machine chest press
e: Elevating the hands keeps the whole body in one line and simply tilts it, which reduces load while preserving the pattern and the trunk demand. Going to the knees also works but removes the hip and trunk position that makes a push-up worth doing.

q: How would you make a push-up harder without adding external weight?
o: Elevate the feet, increasing the share of bodyweight over the hands
Widen the hands as far as possible
Increase the repetitions only
Hold the top position
e: Tilting the body the other way shifts more mass toward the shoulders. It is the same adjustment as the regression, run in reverse, which is why hand and foot height is the main dial on any press-up variation.

q: A client cannot do a single pull-up. Which progression preserves the movement best?
o: Band-assisted pull-ups or slow eccentric-only lowers from the top
Lat pulldowns exclusively
Bicep curls to build arm strength
Isometric holds at the bottom
e: Both options keep the actual movement and reduce the load or use only the strong phase. A pulldown is a reasonable supplement but never requires moving bodyweight, which is the specific capacity being built.

q: What is the standard regression when a client cannot squat to depth without rounding?
o: Squat to a box set at the depth they can control
Add weight to force better position
Squat on an unstable surface
Increase the repetitions at partial depth
e: A box gives an unambiguous target and stops the descent before the spine gives way. It also lets depth be lowered a little at a time, which turns depth into a progression rather than a pass or fail.

q: What makes a deadlift easier without reducing the weight on the bar?
o: Starting from an elevated position, such as a rack pull
Starting from a deficit
Using a wider grip
Holding at the top for longer
e: Raising the start shortens the range and skips the hardest part off the floor, where the leverages are worst. Standing on a plate does the reverse, which is why a deficit is the harder variant rather than the easier one.

q: A client cannot hold a plank with a neutral spine for more than a few seconds. What do you change first?
o: Raise the hands onto a bench, shortening the lever
Add a weight to the back
Extend the hold time and accept the sagging
Move to a side plank instead
e: Shortening the lever reduces the demand while the position is still being held correctly. Accepting a poor position trains the compensation rather than the muscle, and time is only a useful variable once the position holds.

q: Put these in order from easiest to hardest: walking lunge, static split squat, Bulgarian split squat.
o: Static split squat, walking lunge, Bulgarian split squat
Walking lunge, static split squat, Bulgarian split squat
Bulgarian split squat, static split squat, walking lunge
Static split squat, Bulgarian split squat, walking lunge
e: Standing still in a split stance is the most stable. Walking adds the transition and the balance demand of each step. Elevating the rear foot removes its contribution and increases the front hip's range, which makes it the hardest of the three.

q: What is the correct progression of surfaces for balance work?
o: Floor, then balance beam, then half foam roll, foam pad, balance disc, wobble board, BOSU ball
BOSU ball first, then progressively firmer surfaces
Foam pad, then floor, then wobble board
Any order, since all are equally unstable
e: The sequence runs from most stable to least. Working backwards down it is a regression rather than a progression, which is why a balance disc to a BOSU is a valid step and the reverse is not.

q: According to the progression hierarchy, what should be the last variable you change?
o: The load
The tempo
The rest between sets
The exercise selection
e: Pace, set length, rest, exercise choice and reducing feedback all come first. Adding weight is the final option because it is the crudest, and reaching for it first hides all the other progress that was available.

q: A client can hold a single-leg stance but wobbles. What is the next step rather than making it harder?
o: Hold the same position longer or add a reaching movement while keeping the foot planted
Move immediately to a BOSU ball
Add a weight to the hand
Close the eyes
e: Consolidate before destabilising. Adding time or a controlled limb movement raises the demand within a position that is nearly mastered, where an unstable surface or removing vision usually collapses the pattern entirely.

q: How do you regress a Nordic curl?
o: Use a band for assistance or restrict the range to the portion that can be controlled
Perform it faster
Add weight to the upper body
Switch to a leg extension
e: The exercise is defined by controlled lengthening, so the two useful dials are how much help is given and how far down the control extends. Speeding it up removes the eccentric quality that is the whole point.

q: How would you progress a glute bridge?
o: Elevate the feet, move to a single leg, then add external load across the hips
Increase the repetitions indefinitely
Add an unstable surface under the shoulders
Hold at the bottom instead of the top
e: Range, then limb number, then load. Each step raises the demand on the same pattern in a defined order, which is what a progression is, as distinct from simply doing more of the easy version.

q: Seated to standing to single-arm overhead press: what is being progressed?
o: The stability demand, increasing from a supported trunk to an unsupported and asymmetrically loaded one
The load on the deltoid, which rises each step
The range of motion at the shoulder
The elbow extension demand
e: The pressing muscles do the same job throughout. What changes is how much the trunk and hips must resist, first the load tipping you back, then the load twisting you sideways. Weight usually has to fall at each step.

q: A client finds a Romanian deadlift uncomfortable in the lower back. What is the most useful first change?
o: Reduce the range to where they can hold a neutral spine, and check the movement is coming from the hips
Add weight to force better bracing
Round the back deliberately to reduce hamstring tension
Switch to a full deadlift from the floor
e: The exercise is defined by the spine staying still while the hips move. If the back is complaining, either the range has exceeded hamstring length or the spine is moving. Shortening the range fixes the first and exposes the second.

q: What makes a carry harder without changing the weight?
o: Holding it on one side only, or overhead rather than at the side
Walking faster
Walking further
Using a thicker handle
e: Position changes the demand more than distance does. One-sided loading adds an anti-lateral-flexion requirement, and overhead adds a shoulder stability requirement. Distance and speed change the conditioning element rather than the stability one.

q: A client can leg press comfortably but cannot squat. What does that tell you?
o: The limitation is probably balance, trunk control or mobility rather than leg strength
Their quadriceps are too weak for squatting
The leg press is a harder exercise
They require a heavier load to learn the pattern
e: The leg press supports the back, fixes the path and removes balance. If the legs can press a substantial load, the missing pieces are the things the machine was providing. That is where to look rather than at leg strength.

q: The lat pulldown is occupied. What is the closest substitute?
o: A band pulldown anchored overhead, or an assisted pull-up
A seated row
A bicep curl
A face pull
e: The defining feature is resistance from overhead producing shoulder adduction. A band or an assisted pull-up keeps that line of pull; a row changes it to horizontal, which trains an overlapping but different emphasis.

q: No leg curl machine. How do you train the hamstrings at their knee end?
o: A Nordic curl, a sliding leg curl or a band leg curl
A Romanian deadlift
A back extension
A leg press
e: Knee flexion against resistance is the requirement. All three substitutes provide it. The other options are all hip extension, which trains the same muscles through their other action and is not a replacement.

q: No bench available. What replaces a barbell bench press?
o: A floor press or a push-up variation
A shoulder press
A lat pulldown
A dip
e: A floor press keeps the horizontal pressing pattern with a shortened range. Push-ups keep it with bodyweight. A dip is closer to a decline press and involves much more shoulder extension, so it is a substitute with a caveat.

q: No barbell for hip thrusts. What are the options?
o: A single-leg glute bridge, a band around the hips, or dumbbells held across the pelvis
A leg extension
A seated calf raise
A back squat
e: The requirement is resistance to hip extension with peak load near lockout. Removing a leg, adding a band or holding weight on the hips all achieve it. A squat loads the same muscle but peaks at the opposite end of the range.

q: No calf machine. What is the substitute?
o: A single-leg standing calf raise off a step, holding a dumbbell if needed
A leg press with the feet high
A seated leg curl
A wall sit
e: Removing a leg doubles the relative load and a step restores the full range. Knee position still selects between gastrocnemius and soleus, so bend the knee if soleus is the target.

q: No cable machine. What replaces cable work most faithfully?
o: Resistance bands, since both allow the line of pull to be set in any direction
Dumbbells
A barbell
Machines with fixed paths
e: Direction is the property that matters. Only a band can be anchored anywhere and pull from that angle. The trade-off is that tension rises through the range where a cable's stays roughly constant.

q: No leg extension machine, and the client needs knee extension work without loading the spine. What works?
o: A Spanish squat with a band behind the knees, or a reverse Nordic
A back squat
A walking lunge
A stiff-legged deadlift
e: Both substitutes load knee extension with the trunk near vertical and no external load on the shoulders. A reverse Nordic also lengthens rectus femoris at the hip, which the machine cannot do at all.

q: Travelling with no equipment and the goal is hip extension strength. What is the best available option?
o: Single-leg glute bridges and single-leg hinge patterns
Bodyweight squats
Push-ups
Plank holds
e: Removing a leg is the only way to raise relative load without equipment. Both options keep the emphasis on hip extension, where a bodyweight squat shares the work with the knee and is usually too easy to be a stimulus.

q: No rowing machine. What trains the same movement pattern?
o: A hip hinge combined with a horizontal pull, for example a bent-over row alternated with an RDL
A lat pulldown
A leg press
A bicep curl
e: The stroke is a leg drive, a hip extension and a pull. No single substitute reproduces the sequence, so the honest answer is to train the components. The conditioning element needs a separate machine.

q: A client has only a set of light dumbbells and needs a genuine lower-body stimulus. What is the strategy?
o: Use single-leg variations, so the light load becomes a meaningful relative load
Increase repetitions into the hundreds
Focus on upper body instead
Add jumping to every exercise
e: Halving the base of support roughly doubles the load per leg before anything is held. That turns light dumbbells into an adequate stimulus for split squats, single-leg RDLs and step-ups, which repetitions alone will not do.

q: Where should a spotter stand and place their hands for a barbell bench press?
o: Behind the head of the bench, hands close to the bar without touching it, using an alternating grip if assistance is needed
At the side of the bench with hands on the lifter's elbows
Behind the head with hands on the lifter's wrists
Standing over the lifter with hands on the bar throughout
e: The bar is what needs catching, so the spotter is positioned to take it and stays close without adding or subtracting force. Spotting the wrists or elbows gives no control of the bar, and holding it throughout means neither party knows what the lifter lifted.

q: What is the correct way to bail out of a heavy dumbbell bench press alone?
o: Lower the dumbbells out to the sides and set them down, keeping control of both
Let them fall behind the head
Drop them straight down onto the chest
Roll them up the torso to the knees
e: Sideways is the one direction that is clear of the body and the floor space of others. Behind the head risks the shoulders and anyone walking past, and letting them fall inward is exactly what a spotter exists to prevent.

q: How should the safety pins in a squat rack be set?
o: Just below the lowest point the bar reaches, so a failed rep can be set down without dropping
At the height of the lifter's shoulders
At the very bottom of the rack
They are unnecessary if a spotter is present
e: The pins have to catch the bar in the failure position, which means just below the bottom of the movement. Set too high and they block the rep, set too low and the lifter is pinned before they engage.

q: How do you spot a barbell back squat?
o: Stand close behind the lifter and, if needed, assist around the chest or under the arms, moving with them
Hold the bar throughout the set
Stand to one side and hold one end of the bar
Hold the lifter's hips
e: The lifter and the bar move as one unit, so the spot supports the whole torso. A one-sided spot on the bar would tip it, and holding the hips does not stop the bar descending.

q: What is the reason for using collars on a loaded barbell?
o: They stop the plates sliding off if the bar tilts, which would send the load asymmetric instantly
They increase the total weight measurably
They prevent the bar spinning
They are only needed for competition
e: An uneven bar is the danger, not a plate hitting the floor. If one side slides while the other does not, the bar becomes suddenly asymmetric under load, which is how people get injured on lifts they can otherwise handle.

q: What is the safest way to fail a deadlift?
o: Keep hold and lower it under control, or set it down before the position breaks down
Release the bar at the top and step back
Drop it from mid-shin height
Twist to one side while lowering
e: A deadlift is the one big lift where failure has a safe default, because the bar can simply go back where it came from. Dropping it risks feet and bar; twisting under load is how backs get hurt.

q: What should a spotter establish before the set begins?
o: How many repetitions are intended, whether a lift-off is wanted, and what cue signals help
The lifter's one-rep maximum
Whether the lifter prefers a wide or close grip
The rest interval to be used
e: A spot only works if both people expect the same thing. Ambiguity about when to intervene is what produces either a ruined set or a missed catch. The conversation costs ten seconds.

q: Why should a treadmill's safety clip be attached?
o: It stops the belt if the user falls or moves too far back
It measures heart rate
It records the workout data
It prevents the incline changing
e: The clip is a dead man's switch. Without it, a fall means the belt keeps running under the person on it, which is the mechanism behind most treadmill injuries.

q: What is the risk when returning a heavy cable or weight stack at the end of a set?
o: Letting it drop uncontrolled, which can jolt the joint under load and damage the machine
Returning it too slowly
Standing too close to the stack
Using both hands
e: The last eccentric is still a loaded eccentric, and releasing suddenly puts a jerk through the joint at its end range. Controlling the return to the stack is part of the set, not an afterthought.

q: A client is pressing overhead and the bar starts drifting forward. What is the appropriate action?
o: Have them lower it under control to the shoulders, since the forward drift means the lift has already failed
Push the elbows from behind to help finish it
Have them lean back further to complete the rep
Have them let go and step back
e: Once the bar is forward of the shoulder it cannot be pressed up, and leaning back to compensate loads the lumbar spine instead. Bringing it down to the front rack is the controlled way out. Overhead lifts are poorly suited to spotting at all.

q: What usually determines the hardest point of a free-weight exercise?
o: Where the moving segment is closest to horizontal, since the moment arm to the joint is longest there
Where the muscle is fully shortened
Where the bar is moving fastest
Where the joint is at its end range
e: Torque is the load multiplied by its horizontal distance from the joint. That distance peaks when the limb or the bar is furthest out sideways, which is almost always where the lift stalls. The muscle's own strength curve matters less than the geometry.

q: Where is a bench press hardest, and why?
o: Near the chest, where the horizontal distance from the bar to the shoulder is greatest
At lockout, where the triceps are shortest
In the middle, where the bar moves fastest
At the moment the bar leaves the rack
e: At the bottom the upper arm is furthest from the shoulder joint horizontally, so the torque demand peaks. Lockout is easy because the bar sits almost directly over the joint. It is why a board press or a pin press allows so much more weight.

q: Where is a dip hardest?
o: At the bottom, where the shoulder is most extended and the elbow most flexed
At lockout
At the midpoint
It is constant throughout
e: Depth increases the distance from the hands to both the shoulder and the elbow, so both joints face their largest demand at once. That is also the position most likely to trouble a shoulder, which is why depth is worth choosing deliberately.

q: Where is an overhead press hardest for most people?
o: Just above the shoulders, before the bar passes the head
At full lockout overhead
At the moment of unracking
At the bottom of the descent
e: Starting from the shoulders, the bar is at its furthest horizontal distance from the shoulder joint and the deltoid has poor leverage. Once it is overhead the load sits almost above the joint and the position becomes a matter of stability rather than force.

q: Where is a lying leg curl hardest?
o: At the start, with the shin horizontal and the moment arm at the knee longest
At full knee flexion
In the middle of the range
At the point the hips lift off the pad
e: With the leg straight, the pad sits furthest horizontally from the knee. As the knee bends, the shin rotates upward and the moment arm shortens, so the exercise gets easier exactly as the hamstrings shorten. Machines with a cam try to correct that.

q: Where is a seated leg extension hardest?
o: At full extension, with the shin horizontal
At the start, with the knee fully bent
In the middle of the range
At the point the hips leave the seat
e: The moment arm at the knee is longest when the shin is parallel to the floor, which is the finish. That is also where the quadriceps are shortest, which is why the last few degrees are where people fail and why the top of the range gets cut.

q: Where is a Romanian deadlift hardest?
o: At the bottom, where the bar is furthest horizontally from the hip
At lockout
At the midpoint
Where the knees begin to bend
e: Hinging forward increases the horizontal distance from the bar to the hip joint, which is what makes the bottom the demanding part. It also coincides with the hamstrings being at their longest, which is why range should be set by position rather than ambition.

q: Where is a hip thrust hardest?
o: At the top, with the hip extended and the bar highest
At the bottom
In the middle
It is constant throughout
e: At lockout the bar sits directly above the hip with the shin vertical, which is where the moment arm peaks. That is the opposite of a squat and the reason both are worth doing: peak demand at opposite ends of the same muscle's range.

q: Where is a pull-up hardest for most people?
o: Near the top, as the chin approaches the bar
At the very bottom, from a dead hang
At the midpoint
During the descent
e: Approaching the bar means the elbow is deeply flexed and the shoulder nearly fully adducted, so both the lats and the elbow flexors are short and at poor leverage. It is why partial pull-ups from the bottom are comparatively easy.

q: Why does restricting an exercise to a partial range allow so much more weight?
o: The restricted portion usually avoids the position where the moment arm is longest
Muscles are stronger when they contract less
Shorter ranges recruit more motor units
The nervous system adapts faster
e: Partial ranges skip the hard part by definition. That is legitimate when the aim is to overload a specific portion or to work around an injury, and misleading when it is treated as the same lift with a bigger number on it.

q: What is a sticking point, stated mechanically?
o: The joint angle at which the demand exceeds what can be produced, usually where the moment arm peaks
The point at which the muscle runs out of glycogen
The moment the nervous system inhibits the movement
The top of the range, where the muscle is shortest
e: It is where torque required crosses torque available. Since required torque peaks with the moment arm, the sticking point is usually predictable from geometry rather than being a mysterious property of the lifter.

q: How does accommodating resistance address the mismatch between load and leverage?
o: It adds resistance as the lift moves into the range where leverage improves
It reduces resistance at the bottom of the lift
It keeps resistance perfectly constant
It removes the eccentric phase
e: A constant barbell load is matched to the hardest point and is therefore too light everywhere else. Bands and chains add load as the bar rises into stronger positions, which is why they are used on presses and deadlifts rather than on curls.

q: A plank gets harder the longer it is held. Why is that different from the other exercises here?
o: Nothing is moving, so the difficulty comes from accumulating fatigue rather than from a changing moment arm
The moment arm increases as the hips drop
The muscle shortens progressively
The load increases with time
e: Isometric holds have one position and one demand. What changes is the muscle's capacity to keep meeting it. That is why a plank is progressed by lever length or added load rather than by finding a harder point in the range.

q: Why does a cable keep a lateral raise hard at the bottom where a dumbbell does not?
o: The cable's line of pull is sideways, so torque exists even with the arm hanging
The cable is heavier at the bottom
The cable engages the supraspinatus earlier
Gravity acts differently on a cable
e: A hanging dumbbell sits almost directly below the shoulder, so its moment arm is near zero and the bottom of the range is free. A cable pulling horizontally still produces torque there, which is why the two versions feel unrelated despite being the same movement.

q: Stationary bike: how should the saddle's fore and aft position be set?
o: So the front knee sits roughly over the pedal spindle when the crank is horizontal
As far forward as it will go
So the knee is behind the heel at the bottom
It has no effect and only height matters
e: Fore and aft position sets where the force is applied relative to the knee. Too far back overextends the reach and loads the back of the knee; too far forward pushes the knee past the foot. Knee over spindle is the working reference.

q: Stationary bike: what does a saddle set too low cause?
o: Excessive knee flexion through the stroke and load on the front of the knee
Rocking hips
Strain behind the knee
An inability to keep the feet on the pedals
e: Never letting the knee open keeps it in deep flexion under load, which is the classic setup cause of anterior knee pain on a bike. It is the opposite failure to a saddle set too high.

q: Rowing machine: what does the damper setting actually change?
o: How much air enters the flywheel housing, which changes how the stroke feels rather than the resistance level
The total resistance, like a weight stack
The stroke rate the machine allows
The distance recorded per stroke
e: The damper controls airflow, so a high setting feels heavy and slow and a low setting feels light and fast. Power output depends on how hard you pull, not on where the lever sits, which is why a high damper is not a harder workout by itself.

q: Rowing machine: what does a high stroke rate with low power output usually indicate?
o: Rushing the recovery and pulling with the arms rather than driving with the legs
Excellent technique and efficiency
A damper set too high
A seat set too far back
e: Power comes from the legs, which take time to apply. Fast, weak strokes are the signature of someone moving the handle rather than the flywheel. Slowing the rate and driving harder usually raises output immediately.

q: Treadmill: why is a one per cent incline sometimes recommended for running?
o: It approximates the air resistance and effort of running the same speed outdoors
It reduces impact on the knees
It prevents the belt slipping
It increases calorie burn substantially
e: A belt moving under you removes the cost of displacing air and driving yourself forward across ground. A small incline is the usual correction so that treadmill pace and outdoor pace mean roughly the same thing.

q: Why are handrail heart rate sensors on cardio machines unreliable?
o: Grip pressure, sweat and movement all disturb the contact, and holding on changes the workload anyway
They measure blood pressure rather than heart rate
They only work at low intensities
They are calibrated for one body size
e: The measurement needs steady skin contact, which a moving, sweating hand does not provide. Beyond that, holding the rails offloads bodyweight, so the reading and the workload are both altered by the act of taking it.

q: Elliptical: what does increasing the stride length change?
o: The range of hip and knee movement, and therefore the muscular demand per stride
Only the calorie readout
The resistance level
The impact on the joints
e: A longer stride means more hip extension and flexion per cycle, which asks more of the hip musculature. It is the equivalent of changing range of motion on any other exercise, and it is routinely left on the default.

q: Stair climber: what does leaning on the handrails do?
o: Transfers bodyweight into the arms, reducing the hip extension demand the machine exists to provide
Improves posture and safety without cost
Increases the cardiovascular demand
Changes the muscles worked to the upper body
e: The point of the machine is repeatedly lifting bodyweight with the hips. Taking weight through the arms removes exactly that. It is the same problem as holding a treadmill's rails, and it is more common because the machine is harder.

q: Glute bridge against barbell hip thrust: what is the real difference?
o: Range of motion, since the shoulders are on the floor in a bridge and elevated in a thrust
The muscles worked are different
The bridge loads the hamstrings and the thrust the glutes
There is no meaningful difference
e: Elevating the shoulders lets the hip start in more flexion, so the range is longer and the glutes work through more of it. Same pattern, same peak position, more range and usually more load.

q: Stiff-legged deadlift against Romanian deadlift: what distinguishes them?
o: The stiff-legged version keeps the knees almost locked and usually starts from the floor; the RDL keeps a soft knee and starts from the top
They are the same exercise under two names
The RDL involves no hip movement
The stiff-legged version loads the quadriceps
e: Both are hinges. The differences are knee angle and starting point, which change how much hamstring length is demanded and how much of the lift happens near the floor. The names are often used loosely, which is worth knowing when reading a programme.

q: Chin-up against pull-up: what changes besides grip?
o: The supinated grip increases biceps contribution and slightly alters the shoulder's line of adduction
The chin-up removes the latissimus dorsi
The pull-up removes the biceps
Only the grip comfort changes
e: Supinating puts the biceps in its strongest position, since it both flexes the elbow and supinates. Most people manage more chin-ups than pull-ups for that reason, and neither version leaves the arms out.

q: Cable crossover against a pec deck: what is the substantive difference?
o: The crossover leaves the path free and the elbow angle variable; the pec deck fixes both
The crossover trains a different muscle
The pec deck allows more range
The crossover removes the anterior deltoid
e: Both produce horizontal adduction. A cable lets the hands cross the midline and the elbow bend as it likes, which adds range and stabiliser demand. The machine trades that away for a fixed, easily loaded path.

q: T-bar row against chest-supported row: what does the chest support remove?
o: The isometric demand on the hips and lower back to hold the hinged position
The latissimus dorsi
The scapular retractors
The biceps
e: The pulling is the same. Supporting the torso removes the fatigue and the spinal loading of holding yourself bent over, which is why chest-supported rowing is the choice when the back is the limiting factor rather than the target.

q: Smith machine squat against a free barbell squat: what is the trade-off?
o: A fixed bar path removes the balance and stabiliser demand, and also removes the freedom to find a natural path
The Smith machine increases stabiliser demand
The Smith machine trains different muscles
There is no trade-off; it is simply safer
e: The track is both the benefit and the cost. It lets the load be pushed without balancing it, which suits some rehabilitation and some isolation goals, and it forces a path the joints may not want, which is the reason it suits others badly.
